tip: A direct object turns 'der' into 'den': 'den Garten' is the thing being designed, so 'der Garten' becomes 'den Garten'.
When a time expression starts the sentence, the verb stays second and the subject moves after it: 'Morgen fliegen wir'.
'Nicht mehr' = no longer. Together the two words mean not anymore, not literally not more: 'er kommt nicht mehr zurück'.
'Noch nie' = never (up to now). It pairs with the perfect tense: 'habe ... gegessen'.
Definite time spans take the accusative with no preposition: 'nächstes Jahr' = next year.
'Den Führerschein machen' is the set phrase for getting a license; German uses 'machen', not 'bekommen'.
'Sich gewöhnen' is reflexive, so 'dich' is required: 'du wirst dich daran gewöhnen' = you'll get used to it.
A noun with no article is negated with 'kein', not 'nicht': no idea becomes 'keine Ahnung', never 'nicht Ahnung'.
Masculine accusative: after 'einen' the adjective ends in '-en': 'einen roten Mantel'.
'Die Universität' – feminine. Nouns ending in '-ität' are always feminine.
'Ins' = 'in das'; movement into something takes the accusative: 'ins Bett gehen' = go to bed.
'Kein' takes the same endings as 'ein': 'keinen Grund' shows the masculine accusative '-en', just like 'einen Grund'.
'Helfen' takes a dative object, not accusative: 'hilft dem Reh', never 'das Reh'.
'Anrufen' is separable: in a main clause the prefix splits off to the end: 'ich rufe dich morgen Abend an'.
'Untergehen' (to set) is separable: in a main clause it splits, so 'geht ... unter' wraps the sentence.
'Versammeln' is reflexive here: 'die Familie versammelt sich' = gathers; the 'sich' is required.
Polite commands put the verb first with 'Sie' right after: 'schließen Sie das Tor' = close the gate.
'Aufpassen auf' doubles the word: 'auf' is both the preposition and the separable prefix at the end: 'ich passe auf die Kinder ... auf'.
Motion verbs like 'ankommen' build the perfect with 'sein', not 'haben': 'ist ... angekommen'.
For most countries and cities, use 'nach' with no article: 'nach Japan' = to Japan.
'Trotzdem' (nevertheless) takes first position as an adverb, so the verb comes next and the subject follows: 'Trotzdem gebe ich'.
The receiver takes the dative with no word for to: 'dem Gast' means to the guest; German marks it with the article, not a preposition.
'Tagesschau' – Germany's main evening news, broadcast since 1952.
'Eigentlich' flags a plan that changed: the intent was there but reality differs, as in 'Eigentlich wollte ich'.
'Neben' takes the dative for a fixed location: 'neben der Haustür' ('der' = feminine dative).
Adverbial connectors like 'deshalb' (therefore) fill first position, so the verb comes right after: 'Deshalb muss ich'.
'Meiner Tochter' = my daughter's: the genitive noun follows the thing owned: 'die Schule meiner Tochter'.
'Gehören' takes the dative: 'gehört dir' = belongs to you, never 'gehört dich'.
'Über' takes the accusative when it spans across something: 'über den Rhein' uses 'den' even though nothing moves.
'Viertel vor acht' = quarter to eight; 'vor' counts down toward the coming hour.
